extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improv teachers, and workshop participants (theatre improvisation)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidelines and exercises for theatrical improvisation: creating believable environments, collaborating on story, playing specific improv games, and avoiding common pitfalls. Material is aimed at teachers coaching workshops and players improving performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid asking 'What is it?' when handed a mime object
rubrics_metrics.description: If one improviser mimes an object, the receiver should name or use it quickly rather than asking 'What is it?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The original problem—naming any plausible object—is trivial; asking 'What is it?' hands your partner a much harder problem (name an object you couldn’t tell by looking). If the mime conveys shape, size and weight, confident improvisers won’t feel put on the spot. Asking wrecks the reality of the scene and invites audience judgement ('How come you couldn't see it was an orange, dummy?').

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse Twenty Questions / don’t accumulate impossible constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: When participants keep adding qualities without defining relationships or naming objects, the set of constraints can become impossible and break the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either maintain the illusion (object guessed or revealed) or avoid piling on attributes that make no real-world referent possible. This parallels improv scenes where failing to define relationships or to name/use objects leads to collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: CJ sweep — cultivate a rich imagined environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Train yourself to 'sweep' the space with your eyes and see detailed environmental elements (furniture, view, textures) to feed scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide a location (e.g., ballroom) and list visible elements, colors, positions, textures. Use open questions in exercises ('What can you smell?', 'What’s on the counter?') and incorporate as many environmental items as facilitate the scene. Even unseen details inform truthful acting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'Estate Agents' to establish environment collaboratively
rubrics_metrics.description: Have two players walk others through a space, pointing out features that waiting players can then use when they begin the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This teaches how to inherit and use environmental elements established by others; instruct the visiting players to try to use the items introduced when they start their scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mischief vs sabotage — keep mischief clever and concealed
rubrics_metrics.description: When one improviser makes mischief in another's space, it should involve concealment and cleverness rather than mean-spirited vandalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the second improviser is merely a vandal, the scene fails. Mischief should be playful and generate discovery that the original player enjoys finding out (not just making them look foolish). This distinction matters for ensemble tone and audience enjoyment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tilting — build a platform then introduce a transformative but non-contradictory idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Sustain a normality (platform) before adding one unexpected idea (tilt) that could not be predicted but does not contradict the platform, designed to massively change the other character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: two strangers on a bench, then one says 'Yes, this was my favorite place to come when I was still alive.' Ensure the partner reacts (avoid equalizing responses like 'It’s a shame we’re both dead, isn't it?'). Tilts should justify change and payoff the promise that someone will be changed by the interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer high-stakes, affecting offers over trivial originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid low-stakes, random offers that surprise for the sake of originality and don't affect anyone; audiences expect drama and change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An original but trivial offer (e.g., pet store sells ice cream) confuses audiences and suggests panic. A high-stakes out-of-the-ordinary offer that prompts a truthful emotional reaction (e.g., werewolf pet or hit-man front) is accepted and interesting. Surprise without stakes is often confusing or asinine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tilts as training wheels — look within the scene for offers
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard tilts are useful to teach beginners how to be affected and play resistance, but experienced players should discover offers organically within the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't rely on a list of 'standard' tilts; use them sparingly and develop the skill to find the 'right trouble for the right hero' from the scene itself or let reactions lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming characters — pros and cons of real vs invented names
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginners often should use real names to reduce cognitive load; inventing names can free players to behave differently and generate plot, but inconsistent name use can break illusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tom prefers beginners use real names to avoid forgetting and panicking; Deborah encourages invented names to expand possibilities. In shows, inventing names is advisable. For formats with actor-swapping (e.g., Standing Wave/Standing Wave/Standing Wave-like games), consistent names help maintain continuity; consider a whiteboard for tracking names in complex formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working together — prioritize your partner and collaborative process
rubrics_metrics.description: Good improvisers give up initiative, trust partners, and focus on making the process enjoyable rather than constantly 'shining' or competing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach ensemble values alongside storytelling: being 'good to work with' fosters better scenes. Resist instinctive behaviors that prioritize comfort, winning, or demonstrating motivation at the expense of the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tug Of War mime exercise — choose to lose to create a good illusion
rubrics_metrics.description: In the mime Tug Of War, pairs should aim to make the illusion look convincing by choosing when to win or lose rather than straining to 'actually' win.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out that without a real rope there can be no real contest; encourage pairs to read partner's intention (do they want to win or lose?) and to take turns winning and losing. The actor who chooses to lose seizes initiative; winning every time undermines story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept that 'losing' can serve the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing to lose, surrender, or be defeated can be an active story decision, not a weakness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies: Hamlet must choose to die; changing endings to avoid defeat misses the story. Ensembles should accept that some scenes require someone to be vanquished in service of drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break negotiation deadlocks — don't sustain endless negotiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Long negotiations often degenerate into restatement and boredom; skilled improvisers break stalemates by finding new directions or abandoning goals with justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandoning a goal can be an effective device but must be justified in-scene. Techniques referenced: Twitching, Topping, Paperflicking, Shoe Shops for breaking deadlocks and discovering 'what comes next.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Word At A Time — prefer two-person collaborative narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: The preferred version has two people collaborating to create one character who narrates events one word at a time; this preserves physicality, risk, variety, and audience engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the Three Headed Expert variant (three people answering a host) because it becomes talking heads, reduces physicality, lowers risk, reduces variety, and pressures players to be 'funny' rather than collaborative. Use Word At A Time to develop story instincts and ensemble technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word At A Time technical rules (pronouns, tense, acting, mirroring, voice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gameplay conventions improve clarity and theatricality: be clear whether 'I' or 'we' is used; present tense is preferred; act out actions; mirror partner physicality; use a narrative voice rather than dialogue with a fictional other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pronouns: make it clear that everything happens to both players. Tense: present tense useful ('I am walking...') though active past is acceptable. Act it out and mirror precisely (use outside hands to avoid barriers). If players fall into dialogue with a nonexistent other, substitute a narrative voice to broaden description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proto-story and pacing — start simple and build enthusiasm
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with a simple proto-story (e.g., 'You go into a forest. You meet a monster. You run away. The end.') to practice pace, physicality, and gusto before expanding into varied stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage enthusiasm: audiences prefer slightly incompetent but joyous play to technically perfect but restrained performances. If a story wanders into nonsense, 'kill' it and start again. Use the form with pairs for better responsibility and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sentence openers and genre to structure stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Starting sentences with verbs, 'Suddenly', or 'I am a...' helps action and platform-building; employing genre (Jane Austen, Shakespeare) imposes conventions that inspire appropriate dramatic choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt players to start new sentences with 'Suddenly...' or verbs to kick-start lagging stories. Genre constraints give players permission to act within recognized dramatic conventions (e.g., violence in bank robbery, subtlety in Austen) which often frees them to play boldly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Game pitfalls to monitor (adjectives, too much too soon, pauses, pointless originality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common problems during Word At A Time and other games include overuse of adjectives, players speaking multiple words to control, long peculiar pauses, and forced originality that ignores collaborators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjectives: avoid long adjective strings that delay story. Too much too soon: players who say extra words or mangle grammar to control the key word harm flow. Peculiar pauses: indicate inability to commit and waste time. Pointless originality: choosing bizarre words (e.g., 'octopus') to avoid being ordinary undermines collaboration; such players may suit less collaborative art forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat improvisation as 'disposable theatre' — accept risk and ephemeral successes
rubrics_metrics.description: Good improvisers take risks, accept that some work will shine only in rehearsal or be failures, and treat both successes and failures with equanimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage players to try things they may later wish were unseen; maintain evenness of spirit, celebrate attempts, and use 'Again!' or restart when scenes go off the rails during practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing Wave — seamless actor substitution while preserving scene
rubrics_metrics.description: In Standing Wave, actors in lines may tap current players to replace them and continue the same scene, situation and characters seamlessly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate from 'Freeze Tag' where new unrelated scenes start; Standing Wave should preserve continuity (same point, same characters). Run the game ~90 seconds or until many people have tapped in; demonstrate procedure first and select an obvious transaction to anchor starters (doctor/patient).
